title: Vayakhel: no fire on Shabbat (Exodus 35:3)
hook: the one Shabbat labor the Torah names is kindling fire; some read anger into it too

segments.voice: Yesterday, wise-hearted women spinning coarse goats' hair for the sanctuary. Your line was wise hearts spin. Today, back to the start of this portion, and one short verse.

Ask someone what work is forbidden on Shabbat and you'll get a long answer: no writing, no cooking, no building, no carrying in public places, and more. The rabbis counted thirty-nine kinds of labor. But open the Torah itself, and almost none of that list is spelled out. Among the very few acts it names, one gets a verse all to itself, right at the start of this portion, when Moses gathers the people and tells them about Shabbat. One short verse, one forbidden act. Lighting a fire.
screen: `THIRTY-NINE KINDS OF LABOR.` → `ONE GETS ITS OWN VERSE.` → `LIGHTING A FIRE.`

segments.voice: In the JPS 1917 translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." Why single out fire, when most labors are learned from the work of the sanctuary? The Talmud, in Shabbat, records a disagreement. One sage says fire is named separately to teach that each kind of labor counts on its own. Another says it's named to show that kindling is treated a little differently from the others. The rabbis left both views on the page. They also read the words carefully: you shall not kindle. In rabbinic tradition, a fire already lit before Shabbat may keep burning. That's why Shabbat candles are lit before sunset on Friday, so the home has light all evening without anyone kindling. Not every reader took it that way. The Karaites, a Jewish movement that read the Torah without the rabbis' oral tradition, understood the verse to mean no fire burning at all, and historically Karaites kept no flame burning in the home on Friday night. Then there's a reading of the heart rather than of law. Some later teachers, among them Hasidic masters, heard fire as anger and quarrels: don't kindle fire in your dwellings, don't start blazes in your home on the day meant for peace. In that reading, Shabbat asks for a day without fire, inside and out, because it's hard to rest in a house where someone's temper is burning.
screen: `ONE LABOR NAMED: KINDLING.` · `THE TALMUD: TWO VIEWS.` · `LIT BEFORE, IT MAY BURN.` · `FIRE AS ANGER, IN YOUR HOME.` · then, large: `NO FIRE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time your temper flared, and name the spark: a tone of voice, being interrupted, being tired or hungry. Picture it coming again, and yourself noticing it, taking one breath, and not striking the match. If you pray, you can ask for patience in your own words.
Vayakhel. The portion where Moses gathers the people and names one Shabbat labor: kindling fire, in all your dwellings.
Your line: no fire today. The candles are lit before the day begins. Day three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: In rabbinic practice, Shabbat candles are lit before sunset on Friday and no new fire is kindled until Shabbat ends, when the Havdalah candle is lit.

chat.says: If you can't light a fire on Shabbat, how do people have candles Friday night?
options: In rabbinic tradition they're lit before sunset Friday; a fire lit before Shabbat may keep burning.
The candles don't count as fire, since they're lit for a mitzvah and not for any kind of work.
The rule only covers cooking fires, so candles and lamps can be lit at any hour of the day.
